subChunks.title: Request-Response Cycle, Headers & Cookies
subChunks.hookHtml: Every time a web application runs, it sends and receives structured messages. Understanding the full request-response cycle — what travels, in what format, and why — makes you a far more effective backend engineer.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The HTTP Request-Response Cycle

A client (browser or HTTP client) sends a request to a server. The server processes it and sends a response. Both have the same structure:

REQUEST:
  [Method] [Path] [HTTP version]
  [Headers]
  [blank line]
  [Body (optional)]

RESPONSE:
  [HTTP version] [Status code] [Reason phrase]
  [Headers]
  [blank line]
  [Body (optional)]

Common Request Headers

  • Content-Type: the format of the request body (e.g. application/json)
  • Accept: what format the client can handle in the response
  • Authorization: carries credentials (e.g. Bearer <token>)
  • User-Agent: identifies the client software
  • Cookie: sends stored cookies to the server

Common Response Headers

  • Content-Type: the format of the response body
  • Location: URL of newly created resource (with 201 responses)
  • Set-Cookie: instructs the client to store a cookie
  • Cache-Control: caching directives (e.g. no-cache, max-age=3600)
  • WWW-Authenticate: indicates what authentication scheme is required (with 401)

Cookies

A cookie is a small piece of data the server sends to the browser; the browser automatically includes it in subsequent requests to the same domain. Cookies are used for session management, tracking, and preferences.

Important cookie attributes: HttpOnly (not accessible via JavaScript), Secure (HTTPS only), SameSite (CSRF protection), Expires/Max-Age.

Authentication Basics

  • Basic Auth: username:password base64-encoded in the Authorization header — only acceptable over HTTPS
  • Bearer token (JWT): Authorization: Bearer <token> — stateless, verifiable
  • Session cookies: server stores session; client holds only the session ID in a cookie — stateful
  • API keys: a secret string passed as a header or query parameter

storyBeats.text: The Academy's network observatory shows every packet travelling between towers in real time. A senior engineer is walking a junior through what travels in each direction.

storyBeats.speaker: Network Observer Tess
storyBeats.text: Every HTTP conversation is two messages: a request from the client and a response from the server. Both have headers — metadata that tells the other party about the message's format, the sender's identity, and caching instructions. The body is optional.

storyBeats.speaker: A real HTTP request
storyBeats.text:
POST /api/spells HTTP/1.1
Host: registry.academy
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGc...

{"name":"Blizzard","damage":300}

storyBeats.speaker: Network Observer Tess
storyBeats.text: The Authorization header carries the caller's identity. A Bearer token is the most common approach — a signed string (usually a JWT) that the server can verify without a database lookup. Cookies are the older, browser-centric mechanism — the browser stores them and sends them automatically on every request to the same domain.

storyBeats.speaker: Network Observer Tess
storyBeats.text: Mark session cookies as HttpOnly (JavaScript cannot read them — prevents XSS theft) and Secure (HTTPS only). SameSite=Strict prevents them from being sent on cross-origin requests, blocking CSRF attacks. These three attributes together represent modern cookie hygiene.

learningObjectives: Describe the structure of an HTTP request and response (start line, headers, body)
Name and explain five important request headers and five response headers
Explain what a cookie is, how it is set, and the security attributes HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite
Distinguish between Basic Auth, Bearer token, session cookies, and API keys as authentication mechanisms
commonMistakes: Sending sensitive data (passwords, tokens) in query string parameters — they appear in server logs and browser history
Using session cookies without HttpOnly — JavaScript can then steal them via XSS
Storing JWTs in localStorage — accessible to XSS attacks; HttpOnly cookies are safer
Confusing authentication (who are you?) with authorisation (what are you allowed to do?)
assessmentCriteria: Can trace an HTTP request from client to server and back, naming each component
Can set correct headers on an HTTP request for a JSON POST with Bearer token authentication
Can explain what HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite cookie attributes do and why each matters
Can distinguish between stateful (session cookie) and stateless (JWT) authentication approaches
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the HTTP request-response cycle as if explaining it to someone who has only used email. What is a header? What is a cookie? Why does Authentication use a token in a header rather than in the URL?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Answer the following based on the concepts above:

  1. You are building a REST API endpoint that creates a new resource and returns its location. Which status code and which header should the response include?
  2. A browser sends a cookie on every subsequent request to the same domain. What attribute prevents JavaScript from reading that cookie?
  3. You need to send an authenticated POST request with a JSON body and a Bearer token. Write the key headers (just the header names and values — no code).
  4. What is the difference between a 401 and a 403 response, and what header does the server typically include with a 401?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Status code: 201 Created. Header: Location: /api/resources/{newId}

2. HttpOnly attribute. Setting HttpOnly on a cookie prevents JavaScript from accessing it via document.cookie, protecting against XSS token theft.

3. Request headers for authenticated JSON POST:
   Content-Type: application/json
   Authorization: Bearer <token>
   Accept: application/json

4. 401 Unauthorised means the client has not provided valid credentials (or no credentials at all).
   403 Forbidden means the client IS authenticated but does not have permission for this resource.
   With a 401, the server typically includes: WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="api" to indicate what auth scheme is required.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
You are reviewing the design of a new API. For each scenario, identify what is wrong and suggest the correct approach:

  1. The API returns GET /api/logout?token=xyz123
  2. The server stores user sessions in a cookie without HttpOnly or Secure flags in a production HTTPS app
  3. The API returns status 200 with body {"error": "not found"} when a resource doesn't exist
  4. Passwords are stored as plain text in the database and compared directly on login
subChunks.modelAnswer:
1. Problem: sensitive token in the URL — appears in server logs, browser history, and referrer headers.
   Fix: use POST /api/logout with the token in the Authorization header or as a cookie.

2. Problem: Without HttpOnly, JavaScript can read the session cookie (XSS vulnerability).
   Without Secure, the cookie is sent over HTTP, exposing it to network sniffing.
   Fix: Set-Cookie: session=...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict

3. Problem: Status 200 with an error body is misleading — clients check the status code first.
   Fix: Return 404 Not Found with an error body like {"error": "Spell with id 42 not found"}.

4. Problem: Plain text passwords are catastrophic if the database is breached.
   Fix: Hash passwords with bcrypt or Argon2 (adaptive hash functions). Never store or compare plain text.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP response header tells the client the URL of a newly created resource?
questions.explanation: The Location header is included in 201 Created responses to point the client to the newly created resource. It contains the URL the client should use for subsequent reads or updates of that resource.

questions.prompt: A cookie with the HttpOnly attribute cannot be read by server-side code.
questions.explanation: HttpOnly prevents JavaScript (client-side code) from reading the cookie via document.cookie. The cookie is still sent to the server in the Cookie header on every request — that is its entire purpose.

questions.prompt: Why is stateless authentication (JWT in Authorization header) preferable to server-side session storage for a horizontally scaled service?
options: JWTs are always smaller than session IDs
The server doesn't need to look up session data — any instance can verify the token independently
Session cookies require HTTPS but JWTs do not
Server-side sessions cannot support multiple users simultaneously
questions.answer: The server doesn't need to look up session data — any instance can verify the token independently
questions.explanation: With server-side sessions, all requests for a user must hit the same server (or share a session store). With JWTs, every request is self-contained — any server instance can verify the token's signature without shared state. This enables true stateless horizontal scaling.
